lesson.title: The Capacitor That Never Gets Warm: Power That Sloshes, Never Spends
lesson.summary: A capacitor stores and releases energy every half cycle but dissipates none of it on average, a fact that follows directly from the 90 degree phase shift between its voltage and current.
lesson.body:
Capacitive Reactance tells you a capacitor opposes AC current the way a resistor opposes DC current, but with one crucial difference: the opposition is bound up with a 90 degree phase shift rather than a simple in phase relationship. Current through a capacitor leads its voltage by exactly 90 degrees, because current is largest when voltage is changing fastest, which happens right as the voltage crosses zero, not at its peak. That phase shift is the entire reason capacitor power behaves so differently from resistor power.

Let the capacitor voltage be v(t) = Vm sin(wt). The current is i(t) = C dv/dt = Vm w C cos(wt), which we can write as Im cos(wt) with Im = Vm w C. The instantaneous power is p(t) = v(t) i(t) = Vm Im sin(wt) cos(wt). Using the identity sin(x) cos(x) = (1/2) sin(2x), this simplifies to p(t) = (Vm Im / 2) sin(2wt). Unlike the resistor case, there is no constant offset term at all, only a term that oscillates at twice the source frequency and spends exactly half its time positive and half negative. Averaged over a full cycle, sin(2wt) integrates to zero, so the average power delivered to an ideal capacitor is exactly zero.

A worked example makes the numbers concrete. Take C = 100 microfarads and drive it at w = 1000 rad/s with a voltage amplitude Vm = 10 V. The capacitive reactance is Xc = 1 / (wC) = 1 / (1000 times 0.0001) = 1 / 0.1 = 10 ohms. The current amplitude is Im = Vm / Xc = 10 / 10 = 1 A. The reactive power, the peak rate of energy sloshing back and forth, is Q = Vm Im / 2 = (10)(1)/2 = 5 VAR, using the same RMS based product Vrms Irms that gives Q = (Vm/root2)(Im/root2) = Vm Im/2. Note the units: VAR, not watts, precisely because this is not dissipation. If a voltmeter and ammeter were placed on this capacitor they would read Vrms = 10/1.41421 = 7.071 V and Irms = 1/1.41421 = 0.7071 A, and multiplying those two RMS readings gives the same 5 VAR, confirming the reactive power figure regardless of whether peak or RMS values are used.

It is worth stating explicitly, because it is the single most important fact about reactive components: an ideal capacitor dissipates zero average power. During the first quarter cycle the capacitor pulls energy from the source and stores it in its electric field as the plates charge up. During the next quarter cycle that same energy flows back out to the source as the capacitor discharges. No energy is converted to heat inside an ideal capacitor, it only moves back and forth. This is exactly analogous to Reactive Power in general, energy in transit rather than energy consumed.

Real capacitors have small parasitic resistances that do dissipate a little heat, but the ideal model used for circuit analysis assumes none of that. Keeping this zero average power fact straight is essential once you start combining resistors and capacitors in filters, because it tells you where in a circuit the real power actually gets spent, only in the resistive elements, never in the purely reactive ones, no matter how large the instantaneous voltage or current across the capacitor becomes.
